title: Clock Quantum Monte Carlo: an imaginary-time method for real-time quantum dynamics
abstract_summary: This preprint introduces Clock Quantum Monte Carlo, combining the Feynman-Kitaev Clock construction with Full Configuration Interaction Quantum Monte Carlo (FCIQMC) to recast real-time unitary dynamics as a Hermitian ground-state problem and simulate it with interacting-walker Monte Carlo. The authors analyze the dynamical sign problem, propose time-dependent basis rotations to mitigate it, provide numerical examples using quantum circuits, and demonstrate a parallel-in-time implementation strategy.
methodology_description: The authors map discrete-time unitary quantum dynamics onto a static Hermitian ground-state problem via the Feynman–Kitaev Clock construction (H = H' + C0) whose ground (history) state encodes the full time evolution. They adapt the Full Configuration Interaction Quantum Monte Carlo (FCIQMC) interacting-walker projector Monte Carlo algorithm to find the Clock ground state by stochastically applying a linearized imaginary-time propagator G = (1 - δτ H) repeatedly. State vectors in the composite system-time Hilbert space are represented by signed complex integer walkers indexed by system configuration and time. Each FCIQMC iteration consists of (1) spawning children to adjacent times using probabilities proportional to oﬀ-diagonal matrix elements and δτ, (2) diagonal death/cloning using diagonal elements and a population-control shift S, and (3) annihilation of opposite-signed walkers at identical system-time configurations. Observables are estimated from equilibrated walker populations (τ > τ_eq) via time-averaged expectation values of rotated operators when time-dependent basis rotations {B_t} are applied. To mitigate the dynamical sign problem the authors introduce time-dependent basis rotations (an interaction-picture-like dressing U'_t = B^†_{t+1} U_t B_t) chosen (in tests) from local single-qubit rotations to make the Clock more stoquastic or quasi-classical. They also exploit time-locality to realize a parallel-in-time implementation by domain-decomposing the time register across MPI processes so that only nearest-neighbor time domains need communicate spawned children during annihilation. Numerical experiments use synthetic quantum circuits (local rotations and controlled-NOT gates) to quantify the sign-problem dependence on rotation angle and to benchmark parallel scaling.
algorithms_used: Full Configuration Interaction Quantum Monte Carlo (FCIQMC)
experimental_setup: Classical simulation on a Linux cluster (commodity hardware). Implementation uses an MPI-based FCIQMC code adapted to the Clock Hamiltonian, storing walkers grouped by time to facilitate annihilation and nearest-neighbor communication. Example numerical experiments: circuits of 11 qubits, 128 time steps (in scaling test), mean walker populations up to ~1e6, various single-qubit rotation angles (e.g., θ = 5π/32, θ = 0.49, θ ≈ 0.098) and variable numbers of CNOT gates. Parallel scaling reported on AMD Opteron 6376 processors.

Iteratively apply stochastic projector via linearized propagator G = (1 - δτ H): for each walker perform spawning to adjacent times (probability ∝ δτ |H_{j,t';i,t}|/proposal), diagonal death/cloning (using pd = δτ(H_{i,t;i,t} - S)), and annihilation of opposite-signed walkers at identical system-time sites

reproducibility_notes: The paper provides a detailed algorithmic description (spawning, diagonal death/cloning, annihilation rules; construction of Clock Hamiltonian; time-dependent basis rotation scheme) and reports concrete experimental parameters (qubit counts, time points, rotation angles, mean walker populations, and CPU platform type). However, no source code, scripts, or data repository links are provided in the manuscript. Practical reproduction would require reimplementing the MPI-based FCIQMC adaptation for the Clock Hamiltonian and the specific circuits; key implementation choices such as exact δτ values, random-seed handling, and some low-level proposal distributions (pgs) are described qualitatively but not fully enumerated, so some tuning/experiment-specific choices would be needed to replicate reported numeric curves exactly.
key_findings: [speculative] Any unitary quantum evolution can be written as the ground-state eigenvalue problem of a Hermitian 'Clock' Hamiltonian via the Feynman–Kitaev (time-embedded discrete variational) construction.

[supported] The Full Configuration Interaction Quantum Monte Carlo (FCIQMC) interacting-walker algorithm can be adapted to find the ground state of the Clock Hamiltonian and thereby simulate real-time quantum dynamics (demonstrated via numerical circuit examples).
[speculative] The Clock Hamiltonian is frustration free and has a spectral gap scaling as O(1/T^2) (T = number of discrete time steps).

[supported] The dynamical sign problem in the Clock+FCIQMC formulation manifests as a critical walker population threshold nc: below nc samples are sign-incoherent and biased, above nc the sampling becomes sign-coherent and converges to the correct result (demonstrated in numerical experiments with small circuits).

[speculative] Stoquasticity of the Clock Hamiltonian (non-positive real off-diagonals in a chosen basis) is a sufficient but not necessary condition for sign-problem-free Monte Carlo sampling; quasi-classical (configuration-number-preserving) evolutions can also avoid sign issues.

[supported] Time-dependent, local basis rotations (an interaction-picture-like transformation) can substantially mitigate the sign problem in practice for nontrivial circuits: numerical examples show the rotated-basis simulation requires far fewer walkers to reach sign-coherent sampling than the non-rotated simulation for the tested circuits.

[supported] For purely reversible classical gates (e.g., Toffoli) and certain Pauli/CNOT combinations the Clock-based simulation shows very small sign-problem costs (authors report nc ≈ 1 behavior for those cases).

[supported] The Clock+FCIQMC approach is amenable to parallel-in-time domain decomposition: demonstrated parallel scaling experiments achieved >95% parallel efficiency with 2 processors and ~70% efficiency with 8 processors on their test cluster (example: 11 qubits, 128 time points, ~1e6 walkers).

[speculative] By choosing an (approximate) time-dependent basis close to the actual evolution, one can arbitrarily reduce the sign problem (in the limit using the exact evolution the Clock becomes trivial), but acquiring such rotations may be as difficult as solving the original dynamics.

[speculative] In the worst case the required walker population nc to remove sampling bias scales exponentially (on the order of the Hilbert-space dimension) and the dynamical sign problem is generally intractable (NP-Complete in general).
results_summary: This preprint presents a method that maps discrete-time unitary quantum dynamics to a ground-state problem via the Feynman–Kitaev Clock, and adapts the FCIQMC interacting-walker Monte Carlo algorithm to obtain the Clock ground state and thus simulate dynamics. The authors analyze how the dynamical sign problem appears in this formulation (manifesting as a critical walker threshold nc) and demonstrate numerically on small quantum circuits that time-dependent local basis rotations can substantially mitigate sign issues. They also show the approach is naturally parallelizable in time and report high parallel efficiencies in their implementation. The work is a mix of theoretical exposition of the mapping and practical, small-scale empirical demonstrations of the adapted FCIQMC algorithm and mitigation strategies.
performance_claims: [supported] Parallel scaling: achieved >95% parallel efficiency with 2 processors and ~70% efficiency with 8 processors for a test problem of 11 qubits, 128 time points, maintaining ~1e6 walkers.

[supported] In examples using reversible classical (Toffoli) gates and certain Pauli/CNOT combinations, the sign-problem threshold behaves trivially (nc ≈ 1), i.e., no significant walker population required to remove bias.

[supported] Numerical evidence (figures) shows a sharp transition from sign-incoherent to sign-coherent sampling as the mean number of walkers is increased for certain rotation angles and circuit configurations (example experiments used up to ~8x10^5 mean walkers in plots).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper does not claim or demonstrate a quantum computational advantage. It presents a classical Monte Carlo method (adapting FCIQMC) to simulate quantum dynamics via the Clock mapping, discusses theoretical complexity considerations (including intractability in worst cases), and provides small-scale empirical demonstrations and mitigation strategies rather than asserting superior scaling or a practical quantum advantage.
limitations: The dynamical/sign problem remains in general NP-Complete, so worst-case costs (number of walkers nc) can grow exponentially with system size and real time.
The method requires a potentially large number of walkers Nw to remove bias; a critical walker number nc must be exceeded to reach sign-coherent sampling.
The Clock Hamiltonian ground-state gap scales as O(1/T^2) (T = number of time steps), implying potentially slow convergence for long time evolutions.
The linearized propagator (1 - δτ H) is unbiased in the τ → ∞ limit only under restrictions on δτ, introducing timestep constraints.
Finding an exact set of time-dependent basis rotations {Bt} that removes the sign problem is as hard as solving the evolution (i.e., in the worst case it requires full knowledge of the evolution).
The basis-rotation mitigation relies on preliminary computation (to construct Bt) and its effectiveness is circuit- and problem-dependent.

The paper demonstrates the approach only on quantum circuits (discrete gate sequences); applicability and performance on general continuous-time many-body dynamics or other physical systems are not demonstrated.

Annihilation (walker cancellation) requires inter-process communication in interacting-walker Monte Carlo; while time-domain decomposition reduces communication, communication remains unavoidable and may limit scalability in some regimes.
The method assumes system operators can be expressed as a sum of a polynomial number of terms (k-local or gate-based); problems lacking this structure may be impractical.
The numerical demonstrations are limited in scope (simple circuits, modest system sizes), so empirical behavior on large, realistic problems is unknown.
[inferred] The effectiveness of simple local basis rotations to mitigate the sign problem degrades as the fraction or complexity of entangling two-qubit operations (e.g., CNOTs) increases.
[inferred] Choosing good proposal probabilities pgt and pgs for spawning (importance sampling) may be nontrivial and can affect efficiency.
[inferred] Constructing useful basis rotations Bt might incur significant computational and memory overhead, possibly offsetting sampling gains.
[inferred] For problems where the number of processors greatly exceeds the number of time steps, blocking/process aggregation schemes are required and may reduce parallel efficiency.
[inferred] The scheme's performance versus other real-time Monte Carlo or hybrid classical-quantum simulation techniques has not been benchmarked.
